             JOINT APPLICATION FOR APPROVAL UNDER SECTION 203 OF
              THE FEDERAL POWER ACT, REQUEST FOR CONFIDENTIAL
                     TREATMENT, AND REQUEST FOR WAIVERS

         Pursuant to Section 203 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”)1 and Part 33 of the rules and

regulations of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or the “Commission”),2

Rhode Island State Energy Center, LP (“RISEC” or the “Project Company”), and Constellation

Energy Generation, LLC (“CEG” or “Buyer,” and together with RISEC, “Applicants”) jointly

submit this application (“Application”) requesting Commission authorization for a proposed

transaction (the “Proposed Transaction”) whereby Buyer will indirectly acquire all of the issued

and outstanding membership interests (the “Company Interests”) of RISEC Holdings, LLC (the

“Company”), which indirectly owns all of the membership interests in RISEC, from Shell Energy

North America (US), L.P. (“Seller”) pursuant to a Membership Interest Purchase Agreement, dated

as of September 10, 2026, by and between Seller and Buyer (the “MIPA”). As a result of the

Proposed Transaction, the Company and RISEC will become indirect wholly owned subsidiaries

of Buyer.

          As demonstrated below, and in the attached affidavit and exhibits of Secretariat Advisors

LLC (“Secretariat”) (the “Secretariat Affidavit”),3 the Proposed Transaction will not have any

adverse effect on competition, rates, or regulation and will not result in any cross-subsidization of

a non-utility associate company or the encumbrance or pledge of utility assets for the benefit of an

associate company. Accordingly, the Proposed Transaction is consistent with the public interest

and should be authorized by the Commission under Section 203 of the FPA.

         Applicants respectfully request that the Commission, consistent with its precedent, grant

limited waivers of the Part 33 filing requirements to the extent that the related information is not

necessary for the Commission to determine that the Proposed Transaction meets the statutory

requirements of Section 203 of the FPA and is consistent with the public interest.4 The Proposed

Transaction is scheduled to close promptly upon receipt of the necessary regulatory approvals.

Applicants respectfully request that the Commission issue an order authorizing the Proposed

Transaction and granting the requested waivers by December 29, 2026, or 90 days after the date

of the instant filing.

 III.       DESCRIPTION OF APPLICANTS AND THEIR AFFILIATES

           A.      Seller and the Project Company

                   1.      Seller9

           Seller operates as a power marketer with market-based rate authority on a nationwide

basis.10 Seller does not directly own any generation capacity located in any FERC-jurisdictional

markets. Seller currently purchases the entire output of the generation facility owned by the Project

Company (described further herein) pursuant to a long-term firm agreement that will terminate

concurrent with the consummation of the Proposed Transaction.

           Seller is a wholly owned indirect subsidiary of Shell plc. Shell plc is publicly traded on the

New York Stock Exchange (NYSE: SHEL), London Stock Exchange (LSE: SHEL), and Euronext

Amsterdam (AEX: SHELL). The issued shares of Shell plc are widely dispersed among investors,

none of which holds (together with its affiliates) a 10% or greater voting interest in Shell plc.

Through Shell plc, Seller also is affiliated with SR Litchfield, LLC, which owns a 20 MW solar

generation facility within the ISO New England, Inc. (“ISO-NE”) region that is fully committed

to third parties under long-term sales arrangements and will remain affiliated with Shell following

consummation of the Proposed Transaction.

                   2.      The Project Company

(nameplate) two-unit natural gas-fired combined-cycle electric generating facility located in

     apparent ownership of 10% or more of Constellation’s outstanding voting securities, Vanguard should

     Commission issued an order related to the FPA Section 205 obligations of public utilities that are
     affiliated with an investor that owns more than 10% of the voting securities of such public utility. In
     this order, the Commission clarified that “the conditions in the section 203(a)(2) blanket authorization
     orders are designed to prevent institutional investors from exercising control over the utilities whose
     voting securities they acquire,” and accordingly, “with the conditions in the section 203(a)(2) blanket
     authorization orders, there is no common control to make those utilities affiliates of each other under
     18 C.F.R. § 35.36(a)(9)(iv).” NextEra Energy, Inc., 174 FERC ¶ 61,213 at P 42, order granting

     203(a)(2) blanket authorization.”). Accordingly, Vanguard’s ownership interest in Constellation does
     not cause Buyer to be deemed to be affiliated with other utilities in which Vanguard holds voting
     securities under its blanket authorization.

IV.      DESCRIPTION OF THE PROPOSED TRANSACTION

provided in Confidential Exhibit I hereto. Pursuant to the MIPA, Seller will sell, and Buyer will

the Company (and, indirectly, RISEC) will become an indirect wholly owned subsidiary of Buyer,

and RISEC will cease to be affiliated with Seller or its affiliates.

closing conditions, including (i) the expiration or termination of the applicable waiting period

under the Hart-Scott-Rodino Antitrust Improvements Act of 1976 (“HSR Act”), (ii) receipt of the

V.      THE PROPOSED TRANSACTION IS CONSISTENT WITH THE PUBLIC
        INTEREST

        Applicants seek approval under FPA Section 203(a)(1) and Section 203(a)(2) for the

Proposed Transaction. FPA Section 203(a)(1)(A) provides in pertinent part that “[n]o public utility

shall, without first having secured an order of the Commission authorizing it to do so […] (A) sell,

lease, or otherwise dispose of the whole of its facilities subject to the jurisdiction of the

Commission.” The Commission has interpreted the “otherwise dispose of” language to include an

upstream change in ownership of a public utility that effects an indirect change in control of the

utility.27 Accordingly, Applicants respectfully request approval of the Proposed Transaction

pursuant to FPA Section 203(a)(1)(A) for the indirect change in control of RISEC.

        Section 203(a)(2) of the FPA further provides that Commission authorization is required

for a holding company in a holding company system that includes an electric utility company to

purchase, acquire, or take any security with a value in excess of $10,000,000 of another such

holding company or electric utility company.

        Section 203(a)(4) of the FPA provides that the Commission “shall approve” a proposed

transaction “if it finds that the proposed transaction will be consistent with the public interest, and

will not result in the cross-subsidization of a non-utility associate company or the pledge or

 encumbrance of utility assets for the benefit of an associate company.”28 As explained in the

Commission’s Merger Policy Statement29 and in Order Nos. 64230 and 669,31 the Commission

examines three factors in determining whether a proposed transaction is consistent with the public

interest: (i) its effect on competition, (ii) its effect on rates, and (iii) its effect on regulation. Under

FPA Section 203(a)(4), the Commission must also consider whether a proposed transaction would

“result in cross-subsidization of a non-utility associate company or the pledge or encumbrance of

utility assets for the benefit of an associate company.”32 As discussed below, the Proposed

Transaction satisfies each of these standards and should be approved without modification,

condition, or further proceedings.

        A.      The Proposed Transaction Will Not Have an Adverse Effect on Competition

        In Order No. 642, the Commission identified two types of analyses relevant to determining

whether a proposed transaction subject to Commission jurisdiction under Section 203 of the FPA

will result in adverse effects on competition: a horizontal market analysis and a vertical market

analysis. The Commission reviews horizontal market power by assessing the market power of the

transaction parties and any of their affiliates that own or control generation in the relevant market.

For purposes of the market power analysis, the relevant geographic market is generally the BAA,

or a recognized submarket thereof, where the parties’ generation is physically located. Applicants

                 1.      The Proposed Transaction Raises No Horizontal Market Power
                         Concerns

         The Proposed Transaction does not present any horizontal market power concerns. The

Proposed Transaction presents a horizontal overlap because Constellation (through its affiliates,

including the Calpine assets acquired in January 2026) owns generation in the ISO-NE market in

which the Project is located. As set forth in the Secretariat Affidavit and its supporting exhibits,

Buyer and its affiliates currently own or control approximately 2,463 MW33 of generation in

ISO-NE, and the Proposed Transaction will add approximately 555 MW34 of uncommitted

generation capacity through RISEC for purposes of the installed capacity analysis. The Secretariat

Affidavit evaluates the resulting combination under the Commission’s merger-review framework

and demonstrates that the Proposed Transaction does not raise horizontal market power concerns.

         Secretariat performed a Delivered Price Test (“DPT”) analysis of the ISO-NE market

consistent with Appendix A to the Merger Policy Statement. As demonstrated in the Secretariat

Affidavit, the Proposed Transaction readily passes the Commission’s Competitive Analysis

Screen. Following the Proposed Transaction, Buyer and its affiliates will have an approximately

10.3% share of ISO-NE installed capacity, and the Proposed Transaction results in an HHI increase

of only 32 points based on installed capacity. The DPT, which finds the ISO-NE market to be

                 2.       The Proposed Transaction Raises No Vertical Market Power
                          Concerns

         The Proposed Transaction does not raise vertical market power concerns. Section

33.4(a)(2)(i) of the Commission’s regulations provides that a vertical competitive analysis is not

required where the applicants affirmatively demonstrate that they do not provide inputs to

electricity products (i.e., upstream relevant products) and electricity products (i.e., downstream

relevant products) in the same geographic markets, or that the extent of such overlap in the same

geographic market is de minimis.36 As explained in the Secretariat Affidavit, neither RISEC nor

Buyer and its affiliates own or control relevant electric transmission facilities in ISO-NE other

than limited facilities used to interconnect generation with the transmission grid that qualify for

the waivers set forth in 18 C.F.R. § 35.28(d)(2). RISEC also does not own or control any upstream

inputs to electricity products, such as fuel supply, transportation, or storage assets, other than its

own fuel purchase and transportation arrangements entered into in the ordinary course. The

Secretariat Affidavit also addresses Constellation’s ownership of the Everett Marine LNG

IV.     FRAMEWORK FOR THE ANALYSIS

        Market power is defined as the ability of a firm to profitably maintain prices above
competitive levels for a significant period of time. The market power analysis of a proposed
merger or other combination of assets examines whether a merger or transaction would cause a
material increase in the combining firms’ market power or a significant reduction in the
competitiveness of relevant markets. The focus is on the effects of the transaction, which means
that the analysis examines those business areas in which the combining firms are competitors. This
is referred to as horizontal market power assessment. In most instances, a transaction will not
affect competition in markets in which the combining firms do not compete. As detailed above,
the Proposed Transaction will, in effect, combine generation attributed to Buyer and its affiliates
with RISEC’s generation in ISO-NE. SENA’s purchase of RISEC’s generation will end at closing,
and SR Litchfield, LLC will remain affiliated with Shell. Our analysis considers the effect on
competition in the relevant markets arising from Buyer’s increase in generation ownership and the
offsetting effect of the reduction of RISEC’s generation ownership.

        Potential vertical market effects of a proposed merger or other combination relate to the
combining firms’ ability and incentives to use their market position over a product or service to
affect competition in a related business or market. For example, vertical market effects could
result if a transaction created an opportunity and incentive to operate electric transmission facilities
in a manner that created market power for the generation activity of the merged company that did
not exist previously. The Commission has identified market power as also arising from dominant
control over potential generation sites or over fuel supply and fuel transportation systems. Such
dominant control could undercut the presumption that long-run generation markets are competitive
and could injure competition by raising rivals’ costs.

        Understanding the competitive impact of a transaction requires defining the relevant
market (or markets) in which the combining firms participate. Participants in a relevant market
include all suppliers and, in some instances, potential suppliers who can compete to supply the
products produced by the combining parties and whose ability to do so diminishes the ability of


                                                   5
 the combining parties to increase prices.                  Hence, determining the scope of a market is
fundamentally an analysis of the potential for competitors to respond to an attempted price
increase. Typically, markets are defined in two dimensions: geographic and product. Thus, the
relevant market is composed of companies that can supply a given product (or its close substitute)
to customers in a given geographic area.

        Our analysis is conducted in the context of the Commission’s orders governing mergers.
In December 1996, the Commission issued Order No. 592,3 the “Merger Policy Statement,” which
provides a detailed analytic framework for assessing the horizontal market power arising from
electric utility mergers (the Appendix A analysis). This analytic framework is organized around a
market concentration analysis. The Commission adopted the U.S. Department of Justice (“DOJ”)
and Federal Trade Commission (“FTC”) 1992 Horizontal Merger Guidelines for measuring
market concentration levels by the HHI.4 On November 15, 2000, the Commission issued its
Revised Filing Requirements Under Part 33 of the Commission’s Regulations,5 which affirmed
the screening approach to mergers consistent with the Appendix A analysis set forth in the Merger
Policy Statement, and codified the need to file a Competitive Analysis Screen and the exceptions
therefrom. The policy was reaffirmed on February 16, 2012.6 Specifically, the Commission’s

terminated with respect to horizontal market power. Both the Merger Policy Statement and the
Commission’s Revised Filing Requirements provide that a screen analysis (or filing of the data
needed for the screen analysis) is not required where applicants do not sell products in the same
geographic markets or the extent of their business transactions in the same geographic markets is
de minimis.7

        C.       Relevant Product Markets

        The Commission generally is concerned with the following relevant product markets: non-
firm energy; short-term capacity (firm energy); long-term capacity; and certain ancillary services.8

        Both EC and AEC are used as measures of energy in conducting the DPT to assess
horizontal market power. Under both measures, the capacity that is attributed to a market
participant is the capacity controlled by it that can reach the destination market, taking transmission
constraints and costs into account, at a price no higher than 105 percent of the destination market
price.9 The Commission in recent years has given more weight to the results of AEC analyses in

         D.        Relevant Geographic Markets

         Traditionally, the Commission has defined the relevant geographic markets as centered on
the applicants and, for transmission-owning entities, on control areas (now BAAs) directly

and Independent System Operators (“ISOs”) generally are default markets where applicable.

submarkets as separate markets;12 in ISO-NE, there are no relevant energy submarkets typically
considered by the Commission.

          E.      Competitive Analysis Screen

         The Competitive Analysis Screen (or DPT) is intended to be a conservative screen to
determine whether further analysis of market power is necessary.13 If such analysis shows that the
relevant entities will not be able to exercise market power in relevant markets in which they or
their affiliates own or control generation, it generally follows that they will not have market power
in more broadly defined and more geographically remote markets.

         As described earlier, the Competitive Analysis Screen measures the HHI changes resulting
from a transaction, and acceptable HHI changes depend on whether the post-transaction market is
unconcentrated, moderately concentrated, or highly concentrated.

         F.      Description of Methodology

         We performed a DPT analysis for ISO-NE using a model that treats control areas as nodes
in a transmission system. Each node has a demand for and a supply of electric energy. The supply
is based on the generators at the node and potential deliveries to the node via transmission links
from other control areas. Each link in the network has its own non-simultaneous limit and cost,
and a simultaneous import limit (“SIL”) is imposed across these individual limits. Potential
suppliers may use economically and physically feasible links or paths to reach the destination
market. In studying these markets, we consider potential supply within these markets as well as
imports from markets first-tier to the markets being studied; thus Buyer’s generation in NYISO is
taken into account. The data sources and methodology relevant to conducting the DPT are
described in Exhibit SEC-5.

          B.       Vertical Market Power

         The Proposed Transaction does not raise any competitive concerns with respect to vertical
market power.

         First, there are no issues related to electric transmission ownership. Neither Constellation
nor RISEC are affiliated with any electric transmission in ISO-NE or other relevant markets, other
than limited transmission facilities necessary to interconnect generation with the transmission grid.
The Proposed Transaction will not transfer control of a transmission system; the jurisdictional
transmission facilities indirectly acquired with RISEC are limited and discrete facilities necessary
to interconnect the relevant generation to the grid.

         Second, the Proposed Transaction does not create control over fuel supplies or fuel delivery
systems that would raise rivals’ costs. Constellation’s Everett Marine LNG Terminal in ISO-NE
connects to two interstate pipelines and a local gas distribution utility. The Commission previously
found that Constellation’s ownership of generation and Everett in ISO-NE did not raise vertical
market power concerns.23 The Proposed Transaction does not alter that conclusion. A portion of
the capacity at Everett is under long-term contract to National Grid, Eversource, and Unitil through
2030 in the peak natural gas demand months (i.e., November through March); and Everett LNG’s
natural gas sendout in the non-peak demand months (i.e., April through October) of 2024 and 2025
was minimal.24 The Application describes a planned permanent release to Buyer of firm gas
transportation rights currently used to supply RISEC, subject to a separate waiver. These plant-
serving rights convey no pipeline ownership or control and no ability to restrict rival generators’
pipeline access.

                                   Data and Methods for DPT

          This exhibit describes data and assumptions used in the delivered price test (“DPT”)
study (“study”). Because the data are voluminous, we provide them in electronic workpapers.
This exhibit has six sections. Section I discusses the study’s representative periods. Section II
discusses the geographic regions and balancing authority areas. Section III discusses
generation resources, including adjustments to generating capacity for seasons, maintenance,
water availability, and long-term contracts. Section IV discusses the load data. Section V
discusses transmission, including transmission pricing and losses. Section VI discusses market
prices.

I. Time Periods

          The study calculates market shares and concentration indexes for electric energy for
ten representative periods during the year consistent with the Commission’s requirements.1
The year is divided into three seasons (spring/fall, summer and winter), and each season is
divided into three or four periods based on NERC on-peak/off-peak definition and peak load
levels. The seasons are Spring/Fall, Summer, and Winter. For Spring/Fall and Winter, the
market conditions correspond to (1) the Top 10% of on-peak load hours for the season, (2) the
remaining on-peak load hours, and (3) off-peak hours. For Summer, the Top 1% of on-peak
load hours also are considered as a separate period for analysis. Each calculation of market
shares and concentration indexes reflects average conditions (e.g., average loads) during one
of the resulting ten periods during the year (e.g., Summer Peak).2

         In order to define the Top 1%, Top 10%, and Peak periods for a given season, we

10% as the one percent and ten percent of the remaining hours in which loads in the destination
market were highest. These periods have spike transmission pricing and plant availability.

and plant availability.

III. Generation Resources

A. Generation Capacity and Ownership

       The study includes generating units located in the geographic region that are connected
to the power grid.

                 1.       Generating Unit Data

       The study uses data for summer and winter capability at the unit level reported in the
proprietary Hitachi Velocity Suite Generation Unit Capacity database.4 The units include all
generation with a status of operating, standby, cold standby, restart, testing, or under
construction that will be online before December 31, 2028 and with a retirement date after
December 31, 2021 (for consideration of whether to include such generation in the analysis).
Generation units online on December 31, 2024 are used in the base price simulations for the
years 2024-2025. For the forward price simulations and the DPT calculations, the inclusion
of plants varies by season. For the Spring/Fall and Summer season, the inclusion cut-off date
is July 15, 2027. This is the date at which if a unit was online before or retired after this date
the unit was, on average, operating during the season. The cut-off date for the Winter season
is January 15, 2027. Hence, the study represents, on average, the period from December 2026
through November 2027.

               2.      Ownership

       The study relies primarily on Velocity Suite for determination of plant ownership.
These data are supplemented from Secretariat data on plant ownership. For Applicants’

FERC Order No. 860 asset appendix data and information from clients. Before calculating
market shares and market concentration, capacities of affiliated entities are aggregated to the
holding company level. We assume that the NextEra-Dominion, Vistra-Cogentrix, Vistra-
Olympus Holdings, and Hull Street-FirstLight transactions have been consummated in ISONE.

               3.      Seasonal variation in capability

       The study uses summer and winter capability data from Velocity Suite. Spring/fall
capacities are the average of summer and winter capacities.

               4.      Adjustments to Generating Capability

       The generating capability figures used for each period are obtained by multiplying the
seasonal capabilities by an availability factor, which is based on the period, unit location, and
NERC Generating Availability Data Systems (GADS) category of the unit. Data from 2021
through 2025 were used because those were the latest available on the NERC web site as of
September 2026. The GADS database provides national average operating information for
generating units by unit type and size range. For example, it provides data for coal-fired steam
units with capacities between 300 MW and 399 MW.

       For each period and each generating unit, the availability factor adjusts for the
following.

   a) Unplanned outage rates by GADS category
       For a given GADS category, the study assumes that unplanned (forced) outage rates
(as a share of generating capability available after allowing for planned outages) are constant
across seasons and generating units, regardless of owner. Based on GADS data for 2021-2025,
the study calculates an equivalent forced outage rate (EIFOR), which measures the share of
generating capability in a GADS category that is not available because of forced outages. The
computation is EIFOR = (FOH)/AH, where FOH is number of forced outage hours and AH is
                                             Page 4
                                                                                           Exhibit SEC-5

total hours available for generation after planned outages (but before forced outages).5

    b) Planned outage rates by GADS category and season
       With four exceptions (hydro, pumped storage, wind, and solar units), the study assumes
that the planned outage rate is constant for all generating units for a given GADS category,
area, and season. For a given GADS category, the share of hours of generating capability that
is not available as a result of planned outages is computed as (POH + POEH)/PH; where PH
are the period hours, POH are the hours not available because of planned outages, and POEH
are the hours not available because of planned outage extensions.

       Based upon planned outages during monthly peak hours each season reported in FERC
Form 714 by BAA,6 the annual outage percentage is allocated to each season. Because outages
are likely to be “managed” to minimize disruptions,7 the average planned outage rates during
peak periods by season are adjusted. Specifically, the planned outage rate for summer season
is set to zero.8 In winter, instead of taking the seasonal average, we take the lowest level of
planned outages during the three winter months. For Spring/Fall, we used the average of the
planned outages.

    c) Variation in hydro availability across seasons and periods
       In general, utilities use hydro facilities to generate energy during the hours when energy
prices are highest, subject to constraints imposed by availability of water and reservoir
capacity. In order to incorporate these constraints, the study proceeds in the following manner.

       First, the study uses EIA Form 923 monthly production data for the period 2020 to

        For each area-owner combination, we calculate average operating rates from 2020

IV: Load Data

       The report uses estimates of load obligations from information available from public
sources such as EIA Form 861 and FERC Form 714 for AEC calculations. The calculation is
performed in five steps. First, the hours in each period are identified based on time and load
level for the destination markets. Second, load “shapes” are calculated so that the annual load
level in EIA 861 data can be translated into a load amount during each of the ten periods.
Third, the annual loads served by state and balancing area are then merged with the shapes to
give the expected load level served in each period. Fourth, when actual hourly load data for
an entity are available (e.g., from Form 714), we use the actual hourly load data. Finally, an
“obligation” amount is applied to each of the calculated load levels.

       In ISONE, the obligations by municipalities such as Connecticut Municipal are
assumed to serve 90 percent of their load. Obligations by investor-owned utilities, such as
Eversource, are assumed to serve 30 percent of their load. Deliveries of energy by marketers
are given a 30 percent obligation, which implicitly assumes that 30 percent of their obligations
are locked in for a year or longer.

       Load growth from the 2024-2025 historical period is based upon forecasted load
growth for total energy reported in FERC Form 714.

       Average load levels are based on two years of historical data, from January 2024
through December 2025. Because EIA Form 861 data are not yet available for 2025, entity
load profiles for 2025 were created by applying 2025 balancing authority load shapes (from
EIA-930 and FERC Form 714) to 2023 load levels reported in EIA Form 861.

V: Transmission

     A. Transmission Network

        The study incorporates a contract path transmission network for modeling purposes.
Transmission pricing between balancing authority areas in each Region is represented by a
traditional contract path transmission network in which the direct physical connections
between balancing authority areas are also the individually priced links from which contract
paths are constructed.

     B. Transmission and Ancillary Services Pricing and Losses

        As specified by the Commission, the study generally uses ceiling prices for
transmission service from Schedules 1, 2 and 8 of the utility’s pro forma open-access
transmission tariff.16 Transmission providers may require transmission customers to purchase
ancillary services under Schedule 1 (scheduling, system control and dispatch) and Schedule 2
(reactive supply and voltage control). Schedule 8 provides the rates for non-firm point-to-
point transmission service. The study relies on transmission prices from tariffs.

        When tariffs are available, we calculate rates for off-peak, peak and spike categories.
Because of discounting and the nature of baseload purchases, off-peak rates are often lower
than peak rates.17 We use two steps to determine off-peak rates. Step 1: When a utility posts
off-peak hourly rates, we use the posted rates. Step 2: When a utility does not post off-peak
hourly rates, we calculate an hourly off-peak rate based on other tariff information. To
calculate hourly off-peak rates, we divide the weekly rate by 168, the number of hours in a
week.

        We use similar steps to determine peak rates. Step 1: When a utility posts maximum

VI. Market Prices

        There are four price series used in the DPT model: Actual Base Price, Simulated Base
Price, Simulated Forward Price, and DPT Forward Price.

     A. Actual Base Price

        The study starts with 2024-2025 real-time hourly prices reported by ISONE. We use
the ".H.INTERNAL_HUB" price to represent the ISONE market price. To the extent real-
time hourly prices are not available for a particular hour, we use day-ahead average prices to
fill in any gaps; in this instance, there are no missing prices. The default prices used in the
DPT model are real-time prices (as opposed to day-ahead) because load obligations and load
destination hours are determined using real-time loads. The following steps describe the
calculation of load-weighted prices and historical/actual base prices in more detail, which
broadly proceeds in three steps.

        First, for each destination, each hour in a given year of the historical period must be
classified by season and period based on the month in which the hour occurs, the hour’s load
level, and the hour’s on-peak/off-peak designation. Second, each hourly price is mapped to a
DPT season and period according to the first step, and we calculate the annual average price
for each DPT season and period. Finally, we calculate the average of two years of historical
DPT prices by season and period to determine historical base prices.

        The     PRIV_ISONE_Zonal           Loads.csv     files    (See    Privileged   Workpapers:
\Confidential\Loads\) are used to divide the three seasons in 2024 and 2025 into three or four
periods based on NERC on-peak/off-peak definition and peak load levels, consistent with the
10 time periods used for the DPT analysis. The load files have hourly load data for all of
ISONE. Hourly load for the ISONE market is calculated by summing up the loads of all zones
reported.

       To define the Top 1%, Top 10%, and Peak periods for a given season, all off-peak
hours are removed. The remaining (peak) hours are ranked based on load levels in each
destination market by season. Then, the Top 1% and Top 10% represent these remaining hours
in which loads in the destination market were highest. The methodology to map each hour to

       The RTO_price.csv files (See Privileged Workpapers: \Confidential\Market Prices\
PRIV_RTO_Prices.csv) contain the hourly real-time and day-ahead prices for ISONE.

       Using hourly prices for ISONE, each hour in the 2024-2025 period is mapped to its
corresponding season (winter, summer and spring/fall) and to the corresponding period (off-
peak, peak, top 10% and top 1%). After mapping each hour to the respective period, the
average of the hourly price by year and DPT period is calculated. Finally, the two years’ worth
of DPT period prices are averaged by season and period to determine historical base prices for
a given destination.

    B. Simulated Base and Forward Prices

       The simulated prices, which are calculated using mathematical software written in
GAMS (see Privileged Workpapers: \Confidential\PASS_FERC\Price\PASSCP05.gms),
estimate where supply and demand intersect in order to determine the price in a given
destination market. The software uses a simplified economic dispatch algorithm to find the
least-cost set of generation resources to meet demand. Demand and supply are based on
measures of load, fuel prices, network topology, and generation fleet data. The simulations
incorporate seasonal differences in load levels, generation availability, and fuel prices, among
other things. Much of the same data are also inputs in the DPT model. Our “PASS” database
contains information on load during the 2024-2025 period, growth rates for the 2027 period,
historical fuel costs for 2024-2025, estimated fuel costs for 2027, transmission network details,
and generation data from the base period through to the future period.

       Two price simulations are run for each destination market: one for the historical period
(2024-2025); and one for the forward test period (2027). The method used to simulate market

                                             Page 14
                                                                                  Exhibit SEC-5

prices for the base period uses historical data and then simulates again for the future period
using forecasted data. The base price simulation uses historical load, historical fuel prices, and
historical generation data. The future price simulation uses forecasted load, expected forward
fuel prices, and future available generation considering expected retirements and new
generation. The difference in the data inputs drives the difference between the simulated base
prices and simulated forward prices. An additional thing to note is that while historical prices
(actual base price) are real market prices that capture the volatility of the market and anomalies,
the GAMS-simulated prices do not capture this volatility. Simulated prices do not factor in
historical prices and therefore do not consider specific market volatility or anomalies to create
similar spikes in the peak summer and winter periods.

    C. DPT Forward Price

       DPT Forward Prices are then the price levels used in the DPT analysis reported in
Exhibits SEC-6 and SEC-7 (referred to as Market Prices in those exhibits). DPT Forward
Prices are the sum of the historical actual prices, calculated using the steps described above,
and the estimated change in price, calculated from simulations (also described above).        The
relevant output between the forward simulated prices and historical simulated prices is the
estimated change in equilibrium price in the destination market. This estimated price change
is added to the historical actual price to create the DPT forward prices used in the DPT. For
example, if the simulated forward price is $10/MWh greater than simulated historical period
price, then $10/MWh is added to the historical actual prices to determine the market price used
in the DPT.

       the Commission or Commission Staff, 83 Fed. Reg. 21,290 (May 9, 2018) (issued by
       Commission May 3, 2018).

2.     Applicants filed Privileged Materials in Commission Docket No. EC26-____-000
       (“Proceeding”). Applicants enter into this Agreement in accordance with their respective
       rights and obligations set forth in 18 C.F.R. § 388.112(b)(2). Notwithstanding any order
       terminating such proceeding, this Agreement shall remain in effect until specifically
       modified or terminated by the Commission or a court of competent jurisdiction.

3.     This Agreement applies to the following two categories of Privileged Materials: (A) a
       Party may designate as protected those materials which customarily are treated by that
       Party as commercially sensitive or proprietary or material subject to a legal privilege,
       which are not available to the public, and which, if disclosed freely, would subject that
       Party or its customers to risk of competitive disadvantage or other business injury; and
       (B) a Party must designate as protected those materials which contain CEII, as defined in
       18 C.F.R. §§ 388.113(a), and (c).

Definitions – For purposes of this Agreement:

       (a)    (1) Participant: as defined in 18 C.F.R. § 385.102(b); and (2) Party: as defined in
              18 C.F.R. § 385.102(c).
 (b)   (1) The term “Privileged Materials” means (A) materials provided by a Party in
      association with the proceeding and designated by such Party as protected; (B) any
      information contained in or obtained from such designated materials; (C) any other
      materials that are made subject to this Protective Agreement by the Commission,
      by any court or other body having appropriate authority, or by agreement of the
      Participants; (D) material that is privileged under federal, state, or foreign law,
      such as work-product privilege, attorney-client privilege, or governmental
      privilege, and that is designated as Privileged Materials by such Participant; (E)
      notes of Privileged Materials; and (F) copies of Privileged Materials. The Party
      producing the Privileged Materials shall physically mark them on each page as
      “CUI//PRIV” to indicate that they are Privileged Materials. If the Privileged
      Materials contain CEII, the Party producing such information shall additionally
      mark on each page containing such information the words “Contains Critical
      Energy/Electric Infrastructure Information—Do Not Release.”

      (2) The term “Notes of Privileged Materials” means memoranda, handwritten
      notes, or any other form of information (including electronic form) which copies
      or discloses materials described in Paragraph 4(b)(1). Notes of Privileged
      Materials are subject to the same restrictions provided in this Agreement for
      Privileged Materials except as specifically provided in this Agreement.

      (3) Privileged Materials shall not include (A) any information or document
      contained in the publicly available files of the Commission or of any other federal
      or state agency, or any federal or state court, unless the information or document
      has been determined to be privileged by such agency or court, or (B) information
      that is public knowledge, or which becomes public knowledge, other than through
      disclosure in violation of this Agreement. Privileged Materials do include any
      information or documents contained in the files of the Commission that have been
      designated as CEII.

(c)   Critical Energy/Electric Infrastructure Information (“CEII”): as defined at 18
      C.F.R. §§ 388.113(a), and (c).

(d)   The term “Non-Disclosure Certificate” shall mean the certificate annexed hereto
      by which Reviewing Representatives have been granted access to Privileged
      Materials and/or CEII must certify their understanding that such access to
      Privileged Materials is provided pursuant to the terms and restrictions of this
      Agreement, and that they have read the Agreement and agree to be bound by it.
      Each Party shall provide a copy of the Non-Disclosure Certificate(s) executed by
      its Reviewing Representative(s) to the other Party prior to such Reviewing
      Representative(s) receiving access to any Privileged Materials. All Non-
      Disclosure Certificates must be served on all Participants on the official service
      list maintained by the Secretary of the Commission for this proceeding.
      (e)    The term “Reviewing Representative” shall mean a person who has signed a Non-
            Disclosure Certificate and who is:

            (1)     Commission Trial staff designated as such in this proceeding;

            (2)     an attorney retained by a Party for purposes of the proceeding;

            (3)     attorneys, paralegals, and other employees associated for purposes of the
                    proceeding with an attorney described in Paragraph (4)(e)(2);

            (4)     an expert or an employee of an expert retained by a Party for the purpose
                    of advising, preparing for, submitting evidence or testifying in the
                    proceeding;

            (5)     a person designated as a Reviewing Representative by order of the
                    Commission; or

            (6)     employees or other representatives of a Party with significant
                    responsibility for matters involving the proceeding.

5.   Privileged Materials shall be made available under the terms of this Agreement only to
     Parties and only through their Reviewing Representative(s) as provided in Paragraphs 8-
     10.

6.   Privileged Materials shall remain available to a Party until the later of the date that an
     order terminating the proceeding becomes no longer subject to judicial review, or the date
     that any other Commission proceeding relating to the Privileged Material is concluded
     and no longer subject to judicial review. If requested to do so in writing after that date,
     the Party shall, within 15 days of such request, return the Privileged Materials (excluding
     Notes of Privileged Materials) to the Party that produced them, or shall destroy the
     materials, except that copies of filings, official transcripts and exhibits in the proceeding
     that contain Privileged Materials, and Notes of Privileged Materials may be retained, if
     they are maintained in accordance with Paragraph 7, below. Within such time period the
     Party, if requested to do so, shall also submit to the producing Party an affidavit stating
     that, to the best of its knowledge, all Privileged Materials and all Notes of Privileged
     Materials have been returned or have been destroyed or will be maintained in accordance
     with Paragraph 7. To the extent Privileged Materials are not returned or destroyed, they
     shall remain subject to this Agreement.

7.   All Privileged Materials shall be maintained by the Party in a secure place. Access to
     those materials shall be limited to those Reviewing Representatives specifically
     authorized pursuant to Paragraphs 9-10.

8.   Privileged Materials shall be treated as confidential by the Party and its Reviewing
     Representative(s) in accordance with the certificate executed pursuant to Paragraph 10.
     Privileged Materials shall not be used except as necessary for the conduct of the
       proceeding, nor shall they (or the substance of their contents) be disclosed in any manner
      to any person except a Reviewing Representative who is engaged in the conduct of the
      proceeding and who needs to know the information in order to carry out that person’s
      responsibilities in the proceeding. Reviewing Representatives may make copies of
      Privileged Materials, but such copies become Privileged Materials. Reviewing
      Representatives may make notes of Privileged Materials, which shall be treated as Notes
      of Privileged Materials if they disclose the contents of Privileged Materials.

9.    (a)     If a Reviewing Representative’s scope of employment includes the marketing of
      energy or the buying or selling of electric generation or transmission assets, the direct
      supervision of any employee or employees whose duties include the foregoing, the
      provision of consulting services to any person whose duties include the foregoing, or the
      direct supervision of any employee or employees whose duties include the foregoing, such
      Reviewing Representative may not use information contained in any Privileged Materials
      obtained through the proceeding to give any Party or any competitor of any Party a
      commercial advantage.

      (b)    If a Party wishes to designate as a Reviewing Representative a person not
             described in Paragraph 4(e) above, the Party shall seek agreement from the Party
             providing the Privileged Materials. If an agreement is reached that person shall
             be a Reviewing Representative pursuant to Paragraphs 4(e) above with respect to
             those materials. If no agreement is reached, the Party shall submit the disputed
             designation to the Commission for resolution.

10.   (a)     A Reviewing Representative shall not be permitted to inspect, participate in
      discussions regarding, or otherwise be permitted access to Privileged Materials pursuant
      to this Agreement unless that Reviewing Representative has first executed a Non-
      Disclosure Certificate; provided, that if an attorney qualified as a Reviewing
      Representative has executed such a certificate, the paralegals, secretarial and clerical
      personnel under the attorney’s instruction, supervision or control need not do so. A copy
      of each Non-Disclosure Certificate shall be provided to counsel for the Party asserting
      confidentiality prior to disclosure of any Privileged Material to that Reviewing
      Representative. All executed Non-Disclosure Certificates must be served on all
      Participants on the official service list maintained by the Secretary of the Commission for
      this proceeding.

      (b)    Attorneys qualified as Reviewing Representatives are responsible for ensuring that
             persons under their supervision or control comply with this Agreement, and must
             take all reasonable precautions to ensure that Privileged Material and/or CEII are
             not disclosed to unauthorized persons.

11.   Any Reviewing Representative may disclose Privileged Materials to any other Reviewing
      Representative as long as the disclosing Reviewing Representative and the receiving
      Reviewing Representative both have executed a Non-Disclosure Certificate. In the event
      that any Reviewing Representative to whom the Privileged Materials are disclosed ceases
           to be engaged in the proceeding, or is employed or retained for a position whose occupant
          is not qualified to be a Reviewing Representative under Paragraph 4(e), access to
          Privileged Materials by that person shall be terminated. Even if no longer engaged in the
          proceeding, every person who has executed a Non-Disclosure Certificate shall continue
          to be bound by the provisions of this Agreement and the certification.

12.       Subject to Paragraph 20, the Commission shall resolve any disputes arising under this
          Agreement. Prior to presenting any dispute under this Agreement to the Commission, the
          parties to the dispute shall use their best efforts to resolve it. If a Party contests the
          designation of materials as privileged, it shall notify the Party that provided the Privileged
          Materials by specifying in writing the materials whose designation is contested. This
          Agreement shall automatically cease to apply to such materials five (5) business days after
          the notification is made unless the Party, within said 5-day period, files a motion with the
          Commission, with supporting affidavits, demonstrating that the materials should continue
          to be privileged. In any challenge to the designation of materials as Privileged, the burden
          of proof shall be on the Party seeking protection. If the Commission finds that the
          materials at issue are not entitled to protection, the procedures of Paragraph 20 shall apply.
          The procedures described above shall not apply to Privileged Materials designated by a
          Party as CEII. Materials so designated shall remain privileged and subject to the
          provisions of this Agreement unless a Party requests and obtains a determination from the
          Commission’s CEII Coordinator that such materials need not remain privileged.

13.       All copies of all documents reflecting Privileged Materials, including the portion of any
          hearing testimony, exhibits, transcripts, briefs, and other documents which refer to
          Privileged Materials, shall be filed and served under privilege by appropriate means
          endorsed to the effect that they are privileged pursuant to this Agreement. Such
          documents shall be marked “CUI//PRIV” and shall be filed and served under privilege
          upon the Commission and all Reviewing Representatives who are on the service list. Such
          CEII documents shall be additionally marked “Contains Critical Energy/Electric
          Infrastructure Information—Do Not Release.” For anything filed under privilege,
          redacted versions or, where an entire document is privileged, a letter indicating such, will
          also be filed with the Commission and served on all parties on the service list. Counsel
          for the producing Party shall, upon the request of a Party, provide a list of Reviewing
          Representatives who are entitled to receive such material. Counsel shall take all
          reasonable precautions necessary to assure that Privileged Materials are not distributed to
          unauthorized persons.

14.       All Privileged Material and/or CEII in this proceeding filed with the Commission,
          submitted to the Presiding Judge, or submitted to any Commission personnel, must
          comply with the Commission’s Notice of Document Labelling Guidance for Documents
          Submitted to or Filed with the Commission or Commission Staff.44 Consistent with those
          requirements:


44
     83 Fed. Reg. 21,290 (May 9, 2018) (issued by Commission May 3, 2018).
       (a)    Documents that contain Privileged Material must include a top center header on
             each page of the document with the following text: CUI//PRIV. Any
             corresponding electronic files must also include this text in the file name.

      (b)    Documents that contain CEII must include a top center header on each page of the
             document with the following text: CUI//CEII. Any corresponding electronic files
             must also include this text in the file name.

      (c)    Documents that contain both Privileged Material and CEII must include a top
             center header on each page of the document with the following text:
             CUI//CEII/PRIV. Any corresponding electronic files must also include this text
             in the file name.

      (d)    The specific content on each page of the document that constitutes Privileged
             Material and/or CEII must also be clearly identified. For example, lines or
             individual words or numbers that include both Privileged Material and CEII shall
             be prefaced and end with “BEGIN CUI//CEII/PRIV” and “END
             CUI//CEII/PRIV”.

15.   If any Party desires to include, utilize or refer to any Privileged Materials or information
      derived therefrom in pleadings, testimony or exhibits to the proceeding in such a manner
      that might require disclosure of such material to persons other than Reviewing
      Representatives, such Party shall first notify both counsel for the disclosing Party and the
      Commission of such desire, identifying with particularity each of the Privileged Materials.
      Thereafter, use of such Privileged Materials will be governed by procedures determined
      by the Commission.

16.   Nothing in this Agreement shall be construed as precluding any Party from objecting to
      the use of Privileged Materials on any legal grounds.

17.   Nothing in this Agreement shall preclude any Party from requesting the Commission or
      any other body having appropriate authority to find that this Agreement should not apply
      to all or any materials previously designated as Privileged Materials pursuant to this
      Agreement. The Commission may alter or amend this Agreement as circumstances
      warrant at any time during the course of the proceeding.

18.   The Parties may amend this Agreement only by mutual consent and in writing; provided,
      however, that a Party has the right to seek changes to this Agreement as appropriate from
      the Commission.

19.   All Privileged Materials filed with the Commission or any other judicial or administrative
      body, in support of, or as a part of, a motion, other pleading, brief, or other document,
      shall be filed and served under privilege by appropriate means bearing prominent
      markings indicating that the contents include Privileged Materials subject to this
      Agreement. Such documents containing CEII shall be additionally marked “Contains
      Critical Energy/Electric Infrastructure Information—Do Not Release.”
 20.    If the Commission finds at any time in the course of the proceeding that all or part of the
       Privileged Materials need not be privileged, those materials shall, nevertheless, be subject
       to the protection afforded by this Agreement for three (3) business days from the date of
       issuance of the Commission’s decision, and if the Party seeking protection files an
       interlocutory appeal or requests that the issue be certified to the Commission, for an
       additional seven (7) business days. No Party waives its rights to seek additional
       administrative or judicial remedies after the Commission’s decision respecting Privileged
       Materials or Reviewing Representatives, or the Commission’s denial of any appeal
       thereof. The provisions of 18 C.F.R. §§ 388.112 and 388.113 shall apply to any requests
       for Privileged Materials in the files of the Commission under the Freedom of Information
       Act (5 U.S.C. § 552).

21.    Nothing in this Agreement shall be deemed to preclude any Party from independently
       seeking through discovery in any other administrative or judicial proceeding information
       or materials produced in the proceeding under this Agreement.

22.    No Party waives the right to pursue any other legal or equitable remedies that may be
       available in the event of actual or anticipated disclosure of Privileged Materials.

23.    The contents of Privileged Materials or any other form of information that copies or
       discloses Privileged Materials shall not be disclosed to anyone other than in accordance
       with this Agreement and shall be used only in connection with the proceeding. Any
       violation of this Agreement and of any Non-Disclosure Certificate executed hereunder
       shall constitute a violation of an order of the Commission.

       IN WITNESS WHEREOF, the Parties each have caused this Protective Agreement to be
signed by their respective duly authorized representatives as of the date first set forth above.
